title: Dividends vs Buybacks: Which Pays You More?
description:
Dividends vs buybacks: how do companies return money to shareholders? A dividend pays you cash; a buyback uses the cash to buy back shares, so each remaining share owns a bigger slice. In the 12 months to September 2025, S&P 500 companies spent a record $1.02 trillion on buybacks and $664.9 billion on dividends. On day one both give you the same value; the differences are taxes, timing and the price the company pays.

Source: S&P Dow Jones Indices, S&P 500 buybacks and dividends, Q3 2025 release (Dec 18, 2025; 12 months to September 2025, the latest release we could confirm).

Our simplified example: a company worth $10,000 (including $100 of spare cash) with 100 shares at $100. Dividend: $1 per share is paid and, in theory, the share price falls to $99 ($99 + $1 = $100). Buyback: the company buys 1 share for $100; the $9,900 company now has 99 shares, still $100 each. Real prices move for many other reasons. Tax: in a taxable account, dividends are usually taxed in the year you receive them, while gains from a higher share price are usually taxed only when you sell; rules vary by country and account type. US companies also pay a 1% excise tax on net buybacks. A buyback only helps remaining owners if the company doesn't overpay. Educational only, not investment advice.

scenes.say: They paid six hundred sixty-five billion in dividends too.
Ten thousand dollar company, one hundred shares, a hundred dollars to give back.
Dividend: you get one dollar, and in theory your share drops to ninety-nine.
Buyback: it buys one share back. Ninety-nine shares, still one hundred each.
Same value either way. But here's the catch.
Dividends are usually taxed when paid. Buyback gains, only when you sell.
And a buyback only helps if the company pays a fair price.
